Three 160px items in a 320px row. The red one has shrink 0 and keeps its width; the overflow comes off the other two.
Starting sizes of 40, 120 and 200px. Equal grow factors add the same amount to each, so the differences survive.

Cross-axis placement. The third item has no height of its own, so only stretch gives it one.
620px of flex-basis in a 480px row. The two red items are already at their min-width and can give up nothing, so the green ones absorb the whole overflow and the row still ends flush with its border.
freezing where there is room to spare

The red items cannot flex, so their widths are settled before any space is shared out. The green one grows into what the row has left over them, not into the whole row. A floor reserves the room it ne

A flex factor is a fraction of the free space, not only a ratio between the items. Where the factors on a line do not reach one between them they take that fraction and leave the rest of the row empty
one item at 0.5 — half the row
two at 0.5 — summing to one, the row is filled

The red item's floor takes more of the row than its factor was due, so it freezes and the rest is shared again. That share starts from each item's own basis, in the proportion of the factors: green be
a floor, a basis of 160px, and three times the factor
a floor, a cap of 112px, and a plain share
Four 40px tiles in a 170px row, aligned to the start of their line. nowrap keeps one line and lets it run past the border; wrap breaks where the next tile stops fitting; wrap-reverse builds the lines
Where the lines sit once they are formed. Each row wraps into two lines and has cross-axis space left over; stretch is the only value that grows the lines themselves to take it up.
One item stepping out of the row's align-items: flex-start. Item 2 takes its own value; the others stay where the container put them.
The two axes are separate. In a wrapping row, column-gap sits between items on a line and row-gap sits between the lines; gap names both at once, rows first.
